{{Short description|Unsolved problem in mathematics}}
{{for|Lehmer's Mahler measure problem|Lehmer's conjecture}}
{{unsolved|mathematics|Can the totient function of a composite number <math>n</math> divide <math>n-1</math>?}}
In mathematics, '''Lehmer's totient problem''' asks whether there is any [[composite number]] {{Mvar|n}} such that [[Euler's totient function]] {{Math|''&phi;''(''n'')}} divides {{Math|''n'' &minus; 1}}.  This is an unsolved problem.

It is known that {{Math|1=''&phi;''(''n'') = ''n'' &minus; 1}} if and only if {{Mvar|n}} is prime. So for every [[prime number]] {{Mvar|n}}, we have {{Math|1=''&phi;''(''n'') = ''n'' &minus; 1}} and thus in particular {{Math|''&phi;''(''n'')}} divides {{Math|''n'' &minus; 1}}.  [[D. H. Lehmer]] asked in 1932 whether there exist composite numbers with this property.<ref name="Lehmer1932"/>

==History==
* Lehmer showed that if any composite solution ''{{Mvar|n}}'' exists, it must be odd, [[Square-free integer|square-free]], and divisible by at least seven [[Prime omega function|distinct primes]] (i.e. {{Math|''&omega;''(''n'') &geq; 7}}). Such a number must also be a [[Carmichael number]].
* In 1980, Cohen and Hagis proved that, for any solution ''{{Mvar|n}}'' to the problem, {{Math|''n'' > 10<sup>20</sup>}} and {{Math|''&omega;''(''n'') &geq; 14}}.<ref name="HBI23"/>
* In 1988, Hagis showed that if 3 divides any solution ''{{Mvar|n}}'', then {{Math|''n'' > 10<sup>1{{px2}}937{{px2}}042</sup>}} and {{Math|''&omega;''(''n'') &geq; 298848}}.<ref name="Guy142"/> This was subsequently improved by Burcsi, Czirbusz, and Farkas, who showed that if 3 divides any solution ''{{Mvar|n}}'', then {{Math|''n'' > 10<sup>360{{px2}}000{{px2}}000</sup>}} and {{Math|''&omega;''(''n'') &geq; 40{{px2}}000{{px2}}000}}.<ref name="Burcsi2011"/>
* A 2011 result of Luca and Pomerance states that the number of solutions to the problem less than {{Mvar|X}} is at most {{Math|''X''<sup>1/2</sup> / (log ''X'')<sup>1/2 + o(1)</sup>}}.<ref name="LP2011"/>
* In 2019 Burek and Żmija proved that any solution ''{{Mvar|n}}'' satisfies {{Math|''n'' < 2<sup>2<sup>''&omega;''(''n'')</sup></sup> - 2<sup>2<sup>''&omega;''(''n'')-1</sup></sup>}}.<ref name="BZ2019"/>
